article_title: Equity-Focused High School Alumni Connections: A Design Guide for Alumni Surveys
citation: Daal, S., Leones, T., & Iwatani, E. (2026, August). Equity-focused high school alumni connections: A design guide for alumni surveys. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/313
title: A nine-step technical roadmap for co-designing, launching, and acting on a first alumni survey
description: The guide structures the whole survey effort as a nine-step technical roadmap moving from pre-design through action. Steps 1 to 3 cover assessing benefits, assessing readiness, and assembling a diverse design team; Steps 4 to 6 cover aligning on rationale and vision, selecting the audience and designing the instrument, and launching; Steps 7 to 9 cover interpreting results, forming actionable steps, and implementing and adjusting actions with feedback loops. The roadmap is based on the authors' multi-year pilots and expert interviews.
requirements: Sufficient leadership and staff buy-in, since designing, launching, interpreting, and acting on a survey takes significant time and attention
Resources including staff time, a secure survey platform, and staff for data cleaning, visualization, and analysis
constraints: The roadmap targets teams designing and launching their first alumni survey
target_learners: District and school teams in K-12 education
target_learning_goals: Transforming alumni feedback into a driver for institutional change
examples: Step 2 poses readiness questions about organizational capacity, alumni capacity, and the ability to use results effectively, including testing the quality of an alumni email list before a full survey.
key_sources: Daal, S., Leones, T., & Iwatani, E. (2026, August). Equity-focused high school alumni connections: A design guide for alumni surveys. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/313

article_title: Talent Development High School (TDHS)- Attendance
citation: Talent Development High School. (2005). https://eric.ed.gov/
title: Ninth-grade structure of interdisciplinary learning communities with double-dose courses and freshman seminars
description: This pattern organizes the ninth grade into "small interdisciplinary learning communities within the 9th grade" and pairs it with curricula based on "double dose" English and math courses. Freshman seminars focus on study skills and time management, and the structure is complemented by career academies and cooperative learning, all introduced through professional development.
requirements: Professional development to help schools implement the structure
An additional teacher-level facilitator is required
target_learners: 9th graders in high-poverty urban high schools
target_learning_goals: English and mathematics achievement
study skills and time management
examples: Talent Development High School schools implemented double-dose English and math courses and freshman seminars as part of the model

article_title: How States Are Expanding Quality Summer Learning Opportunities
citation: Fitz, J., Woods, J., Duran, N., & McCombs, J. (2025). How states are expanding quality summer learning opportunities. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/910.329
title: State summer learning grant programs profiled in the nine case study states
description: The report profiles state grant programs including Georgia's BOOST, Louisiana's Jump Start and ESSER grants, Massachusetts's ASOST family, Michigan's Out-of-School Time grant, New Mexico's Summer Enrichment Internship Program, Oregon's Summer Learning Grants, Tennessee's Learning Loss Remediation and Student Acceleration Act, Texas's Additional Days School Year, and Vermont's Summer Matters for All and Act 78 programs. Programs varied in grantees (LEAs vs. CBOs), funding sources, and goals; for example, BOOST's 97 grantees served "nearly 87,000 youth, which represented 5% of Georgia's K–12 student population" in summer 2023.

constraints: As of September 2024, states will have spent or obligated all ARPA ESSER funds, prompting sustainability decisions
target_learners: K-12 students, with some programs targeting high school students ages 16–18
target_learning_goals: academic learning and enrichment
career development
support for working families
examples: Tennessee reported over 201,000 students attended summer learning camps in 2023, representing 20% of the state's K–12 student population

article_title: Detecting GPT-Assisted Writing Using Interpretable Stylometric Features
citation: Rajesh Kumar, Nabeel Siddiqui, Alexander Fuchsberger. (2026). Detecting GPT-Assisted Writing Using Interpretable Stylometric Features. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26687
title: Nine-feature interpretable stylometric representation of writing samples
description: Each writing sample is represented by "nine interpretable lexical, syntactic, and sentence-level features that quantify vocabulary diversity, vocabulary richness, grammatical composition, and sentence-length variation": Type-Token Ratio, Hapax Ratio, Word Entropy, Non-stopword Ratio, Noun, Verb, Adjective, and Adverb ratios, and Sentence-Length Variability. Unlike proprietary prediction scores or latent neural embeddings, these features correspond to explicit linguistic characteristics that educators and integrity investigators can independently examine.
requirements: Computed per fixed-length window with centering and scaling parameters estimated from training data only
constraints: Lexical-diversity measures can be influenced by document length, which the windowing design addresses
target_learning_goals: characterizing writing style through observable lexical and grammatical evidence
examples: Features were extracted using quanteda for tokenization and the udpipe English EWT model for part-of-speech annotation

article_title: Systematic Review of Collaborative Learning Activities for Promoting AI Literacy
citation: A Hingle, A Johri. (2024). Systematic Review of Collaborative Learning Activities for Promoting AI Literacy. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6178-1256
title: Corpus of nine empirical studies of collaborative learning for AI literacy (2015-2023)
description: A systematically collected corpus of nine studies published between January 2015 and December 2023, identified via PRISMA procedures from ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, SCOPUS, and Web of Science, with an initial yield of 227 studies. Studies span classroom, online community, home, office, and crowdsourced settings and audiences from children (ages 7-12) to educators, families, pathologists, and undergraduate computing students. Inter-rater agreement for inclusion and exclusion criteria was 0.9 (Cohen's kappa). Table 1 summarizes each study's goal, location, activity, and participants.
requirements: Studies had to meet six criteria: 2015-2023 publication, conference or journal venue, English, AI literacy focus, human-human or human-AI collaboration, and an empirical activity or intervention
constraints: ScienceDirect and ProQuest were excluded due to excessive irrelevant studies; the final dataset may potentially exclude relevant studies using different descriptors
target_learning_goals: AI literacy
machine learning literacy
21st century skills
human-AI collaboration competence
technical AI skills
examples: Included studies include Druga et al. 2019 (102 children, workshops across four countries), Lee et al. 2022 (37 educators in an AI book club), and Cai et al. 2019 (21 pathologists in a qualitative laboratory study)
key_sources: A Hingle, A Johri. (2024). Systematic Review of Collaborative Learning Activities for Promoting AI Literacy. https://orcid.org/0000-0002-6178-1256

article_title: An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria
citation: Nwogo, E. U., Ihianle, I. K., Machado, P., Bird, J. J., Lotfi, A., Shuaib, A. A., Akinwumi, I. I., & Oluranti, J. (2026). An AI-Based Adaptive Learning Platform for Multilingual and Low-Resource Educational Contexts: A Case Study on Nigeria. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.15738
title: Curated Nigerian Pidgin English corpus of 416,343 text entries scraped from BBC Pidgin and Prime9ja, publicly released for fine-tuning and evaluation
description: A web-scraped corpus of Nigerian Pidgin English built from publicly accessible news platforms including BBC Pidgin and Prime9ja, cleaned through lowercasing, deduplication and normalisation, and formatted into instruction-style conversational pairs. The authors state "the final dataset comprises 416,343 high-quality Nigerian Pidgin English text entries spanning news reporting, commentary, and informal discourse". It was used to fine-tune the platform's Pidgin-aware LLM and released publicly via Zenodo and Hugging Face.
requirements: Responsible scraping practices as described: public content only, exclusion of user-restricted pages, and request rate-limiting
constraints: Sourced from informal news reporting and commentary, encompassing narrative, conversational, and domain-specific expressions rather than curated pedagogical text
target_learners: Nigerian learners in multilingual, low-resource educational contexts
target_learning_goals: Linguistic alignment of AI-generated instructional content in Nigerian Pidgin English
examples: The corpus was tokenised with AutoTokenizer and used to fine-tune a LLaMA-based instruction model via LoRA

article_title: Structured AI Demonstrations and Student LLM Use in Engineering Mechanics: Study Design and Preliminary Results
citation: Shuang Geng, Helen Lallos-Harrell, Jiya Ashar, Thomas J. McKenna, Annwesa Dasgupta, Caleb Farny, and Emma Lejeune. (2026). Structured AI Demonstrations and Student LLM Use in Engineering Mechanics: Study Design and Preliminary Results. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28710
title: Sequence of nine structured instructor-led AI demonstrations for modeling strategic LLM delegation and evaluation
description: A deployable classroom intervention: nine short, instructor-led AI demonstrations delivered at roughly weekly cadence, progressing from baseline tool literacy through pedagogical framing (metacognition, Socratic tutor system prompts), strategic delegation of low-risk programming tasks for a truss design project, and LLM benchmarking. As the article states, "Each demonstration occupied approximately 10–15 minutes at the end of a regularly scheduled class meeting and recurred at roughly weekly cadence." Demonstration workflows and the Socratic tutor system prompt are publicly documented in appendices.
requirements: Delivered by the regular course instructor within existing lecture time without displacing core content
Complete workflows and system prompt are documented and reproducible from the published appendices
constraints: Demonstrations evolved dynamically by instructor judgment rather than a rigid script, so components driving outcomes cannot be isolated
Some timing was misaligned with student readiness and end-of-semester fatigue affected later sessions
target_learners: undergraduate engineering students in a core problem-solving course
target_learning_goals: strategic LLM delegation
model evaluation and benchmarking
metacognitive awareness of AI's role in learning
examples: Demonstration 4 used a custom system prompt converting a general-purpose LLM into an EK301 Socratic tutor; Demonstrations 5-6 showed strategic delegation of GUI building and optimization routines for the truss project

article_title: A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI
citation: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518
title: Nine-check verification-and-validation repertoire (V1–V9) for classroom sensemaking
description: The article operationalizes the sensemaking pillar as a cumulative repertoire of nine checks scaled from professional verification, validation, and uncertainty quantification: units and dimensions, order of magnitude, known-answer checks, self-consistency, convergence, conservation, independence, limiting cases, and comparison with experiment. Each check enters at a particular rung of the task progression and remains required thereafter. The author emphasizes that "every check in this repertoire is physics or mathematics content, not programming content," that the checks are cumulative and cheap, and that they bound rather than close the space of undetected errors.
requirements: Checks must be enforced as course culture; the article argues their low cost is what makes them enforceable rather than aspirational policy.
constraints: The checks bound, but do not close, the space of undetected errors; stronger code verification by manufactured solutions requires contributory code expertise the course deliberately does not build, and when the agent executes the checks, each check inherits the trust problem of the system under test.
target_learners: undergraduate physics students across the computational progression
target_learning_goals: sensemaking and verification of computational outputs in physics
examples: V3 known-answer check: integrate x^2 before e^-x^2; simulate the drag-free projectile before adding drag. V7 independence distinguishes a genuinely different method (gold standard) from re-querying the agent (weakest, correlated samples).
key_sources: Larry Engelhardt. (2026). A Tool-Invariant Framework for Teaching and Assessing Computational Methods in the Age of Agentic AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15518

article_title: Guidelines for Designing AI Technologies to Support Adult Learning
citation: Jennifer M. Reddig, Glen R. Smith Jr., Sanaz Ahmadzadeh Siyahrood, Wesley G. Morris, Yoojin Bae, Kaitlyn Crutcher, John Kos, Rahul K. Dass, Jinho Kim, Momin Naushad Siddiqui, Daniel Weitekamp, Ploy Thajchayapong, Sandeep Kakar, Alex Endert, Scott Crossley, Min Kyu Kim, Chris Dede, Ashok Goel, and Christopher J. MacLellan. 2026. title: Nineteen empirically grounded design guidelines for AI-powered adult learning technologies
description: The article distills longitudinal deployment data into "a set of 19 design guidelines intended to inform future AI-supported adult learning technologies", each framed as an actionable statement beginning with "AI tools should...". Each guideline is annotated with the Community of Inquiry dimension it supports, the immediately impacted stakeholders, and the technology problems it mitigates (e.g., access, trust, low engagement, low learning). The guidelines range from data governance (G1) and accessibility (G2) to personalization (G11), contextualized help (G13), and fostering community (G19).

constraints: The authors acknowledge another research team, drawing on different experiences and values, might arrive at an alternate set of themes or guidelines when analyzing the same dataset

Instructors and administrators in adult education

article_title: Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks
citation: Nilsen P. (2015). Making sense of implementation theories, models and frameworks. Implementation Science. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13012-015-0242-0
title: Taxonomy of five categories of theoretical approaches in implementation science organized by three overarching aims
description: The article proposes a taxonomy that distinguishes five categories of theoretical approaches used in implementation science: process models, determinant frameworks, classic theories, implementation theories and evaluation frameworks. These map onto three overarching aims: "describing and/or guiding the process of translating research into practice", "understanding and/or explaining what influences implementation outcomes", and "evaluating implementation". The second aim is further broken down into determinant frameworks, classic theories and implementation theories based on origins, development, knowledge sources, stated aims and applications.
requirements: Users must recognize that the categories differ in assumptions, aims and characteristics, which have implications for their use
constraints: The categories are not always recognized as separate types of approaches in the literature, and there is considerable overlap between some of the categories
target_learning_goals: selecting appropriate theoretical approaches for implementation research and practice
examples: Table 1 lists the five categories with descriptions and examples such as the Knowledge-to-Action Model, PARIHS, CFIR, COM-B and RE-AIM

article_title: A Game Design Methodology for Generating a Psychological Profile of Players
citation: Guardiola, E., & Natkin, S. (2015). A Game Design Methodology for Generating a Psychological Profile of Players. In Serious Games Analytics, Methodologies for Performance Measurement, Assessment, and Improvement. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-05834-4
title: Nine-step game design methodology for generating a psychological profile of players
description: The article proposes a game design process dedicated to psychological profiling, stating: "Following our framework, we propose a game design process in 9 steps". The steps cover selecting a validated psychological model, setting audience constraints, building an expert validation pipeline, confronting the player model with the psychological model, defining psychometric items inside the gameplay loop, rationalizing content-dimension links, documenting the results interface, running a test-and-analysis protocol, and iterating. Its originality lies in the coexistence of the player model and the psychological model throughout design.
requirements: A scientifically validated psychological model with a referential test for comparison
A pipeline for content validation by domain experts
A documented interface explaining how gameplay elements become items and how the profile is calculated
A test and analysis protocol comparing game results with a classical questionnaire
constraints: The article reports the method applied in one serious game production with timing and budget constraints; validation of psychometric use was not the goal of the first test session
target_learners: vocational guidance audiences from middle school students to adults in career change
target_learning_goals: assessment of vocational interests, motivation and decision style through gameplay
examples: The method was applied step by step during the development of JEU SERAI, a serious game using 18 mini games mapped to Holland RIASEC types

article_title: Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age
citation: Daniel L. Schwartz and Dylan Arena. (2013). Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age. The MIT Press. http://www.macfound.org
title: Design nimble choice-based assessments that stand independently of specific instructional packages
description: The report argues for smaller, more nimble choice-based assessments rather than bulky environments like cognitive tutors or full video games. Nimble assessments "do not depend on students completing many hours of a complex game or instructional sequence before it is possible to make any useful assessments." They can target specific choices by design, be built by many people to democratize assessment design, allow the same constellation of choices to be assessed with several measures, and stand independently of a specific instructional package so different learning experiences can be compared.
requirements: Assessment design must target specific choices rather than search for diagnostic patterns among millions of choice combinations in open environments
constraints: The authors note the results from a single, monolithic assessment are questionable because they may reflect unknown peculiarities of the environment
target_learners: Learners in formal and informal settings, including museum visitors
target_learning_goals: Assessing choices critical to learning that most tests miss
examples: The Ohno! Has Talent choicelet is offered as a modest illustration of a nimble, choice-based assessment of critical thinking
key_sources: Daniel L. Schwartz and Dylan Arena. (2013). Measuring What Matters Most: Choice-Based Assessments for the Digital Age. The MIT Press. http://www.macfound.org

article_title: The development of inhibitory control in adolescence and prospective relations with delinquency
citation: Fosco, W. D., Hawk, L. W. Jr., Colder, C. R., Meisel, S. N., & Lengua, L. J. (2019). The development of inhibitory control in adolescence and prospective relations with delinquency. Journal of Adolescence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.adolescence.2019.08.008
title: Nigg's framework distinguishing inhibitory control from self-regulation and impulsivity
description: The article adopts Nigg's (2017) framework in which self-regulation is "a broad, domain-general ability to flexibly and adaptively modulate one's own behavior and internal states," while inhibitory control (response inhibition) involves preventing or stopping an ongoing response and is a building block for more complex cognitive functions. Impulsivity differs in that it "entails disinhibition in the context of valenced stimuli" and prioritizes immediate over delayed consequences, whereas inhibitory control does not consider motivational context. The study uses this framework to justify measuring inhibitory control with both a task and a questionnaire.
requirements: Assessment tools must be selected to match the construct as defined: tasks capture inhibition in a cold cognitive context, questionnaires capture inhibition across motivated everyday contexts
constraints: Questionnaire measures of inhibitory control overlap somewhat with impulsivity measures because items reflect inhibition in contexts with motivation to respond
target_learning_goals: self-regulation and inhibitory control development
examples: The study operationalized the framework with the Stop Signal Task for task-based inhibitory control and the EATQ-R inhibitory control subscale for questionnaire-based inhibitory control

article_title: Toward a classification of discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions
citation: Fu, E. L. F., van Aalst, J., & Chan, C. K. K. (2016). Toward a classification of discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 11, 441-478. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9245-3
title: Nine discourse patterns classified into three modes of online discourse: knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge building
description: The study developed a classification of nine discourse patterns that occur in text-based asynchronous discussion forums, organized under van Aalst's (2009) three-mode framework. Knowledge sharing comprises five patterns (fact-oriented, cumulative, repetitive, simple argumentation, disputational); knowledge construction comprises two (explanatory and problem-centered inquiry, complex argumentation); knowledge building comprises two (progressive inquiry, sustained discourse for community advance). The authors state the goal was to Bdevelop a classification for a range of discourse patterns that occur in text-based asynchronous discussionforums, and that can aid in the distinction of three modes of discourse: knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge building.
requirements: Qualitative coding and narrative analysis of inquiry threads in Knowledge Forum databases
constraints: Patterns were identified from three discussion views in one professional development project in Hong Kong; generalizability to other contexts is not established in the text provided
target_learners: Grade 5 and Grade 10 students in Knowledge Building Teacher Network classrooms
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge building in collaborative online discourse
key_sources: Fu, E. L. F., van Aalst, J., & Chan, C. K. K. (2016). Toward a classification of discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 11, 441-478. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9245-3

article_title: A Systematic Review of Evidence-Based Wellbeing Initiatives for Schoolteachers and Early Childhood Educators
citation: Emily Berger, Andrea Reupert, Timothy C. H. Campbell, Zoe Morris, Marie Hammer, Zane Diamond, Rochelle Hine, Pamela Patrick, Chantel Fathers. (2022). A Systematic Review of Evidence-Based Wellbeing Initiatives for Schoolteachers and Early Childhood Educators. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-022-09690-5
title: Nineteen educator wellbeing initiatives organised into six therapeutic categories plus school leadership and policy change
description: The review's central artifact is a structured inventory of 19 distinct educator wellbeing initiatives drawn from 23 studies, organised by therapeutic approach: "The six therapeutic categories of "mindfulness", "social-emotional", "mental health literacy", "cognitive behavioural", "positive psychology", and "integrative" were used to organise the results", with a final non-therapeutic category of school leadership and policy change. target_learning_goals: educator wellbeing, stress reduction, mental health literacy and resilience
examples: Seven initiatives were mindfulness-based, five social-emotional, two mental health literacy, one positive psychology, one school leadership and policy change, one cognitive behavioural, and two integrative

article_title: The process of tool innovation in young children: An attempt to bridge the Gestalt and the perception-action theories
citation: Guo, J.; Bai, H.; Long, X.; Su, X.; Pang, W. (2025). The process of tool innovation in young children: An attempt to bridge the Gestalt and the perception-action theories. Learning and Instruction, 99, article 102182. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2025.102182
title: Nine tool innovation tasks spanning three paradigms and three tool types
description: A validated task battery for studying tool innovation in 3- to 6-year-olds: "nine tasks spanning three tool innovation test paradigms (Hook task, Push task, and Cling task) and three types of tools (add, subtract, and reshape)". Each task has one intended manipulation and a warm-up with exercise materials manipulable in the same way. The new Cling Task requires retrieving a reward from an upstanding tube through clinging. Performance is coded as task success and ideal manipulation, and the exploration process is coded for fixation and flexibility behaviors.
requirements: A warm-up session familiarizing children with the manipulative actions
Prompts such as "please try another way" when children repeatedly use an ineffective strategy
Two trained coders per child for reliability
constraints: The Cling-subtract task showed a low factor loading (0.17) on task success and is subject to further improvement
Task order was only partially counterbalanced
target_learning_goals: tool innovation
creativity
problem solving
examples: Children were tested individually in kindertartens in two 20–30 minute sessions; inter-coder ICCs ranged from 0.69 (fixation) to 1.00 (task success).

article_title: Understanding the structure of the set of rational numbers: a conceptual change approach
citation: Xenia Vamvakoussi, Stella Vosniadou. (2004). Understanding the structure of the set of rational numbers: a conceptual change approach. Learning and Instruction. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190233
title: Empirical study of ninth graders' understanding of algebraic and structural properties of rational numbers
description: The article reports an empirical study in which the authors "investigated ninth graders' understanding of algebraic and structural properties of rational numbers, from a conceptual change perspective". The study examined which aspects of rational-number structure prior natural-number knowledge supports and which are constrained by the presupposition of discreteness, grounding the article's conceptual change argument for mathematics.
requirements: Investigates students' understanding from a conceptual change perspective, as the article states.
target_learning_goals: algebraic and structural properties of rational numbers, including density
examples: The study's findings are that prior natural-number knowledge supports algebraic properties while discreteness constrains density understanding.

article_title: Criteria to Employ in Choice of Tests.
citation: Franzen, R., & Knight, F. B. (1921). Criteria to Employ in Choice of Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology.
title: Nine-criterion framework for judging the value of educational tests
description: The article enumerates nine virtues a test may possess to varying degrees, from validity ('Measure what it purports to measure') through reliability, objectivity, scaling, norms, interest to the child, range of abilities registered, diagnostic discrimination between failures, and correlation with intelligence at maximum ability. The framework is offered as 'a convenient assembly of important test virtues' to guide administrators who must choose among many existing tests rather than find one.
requirements: Tests must be evaluated against all nine virtues before selection, with published data such as correlation with a criterion, reliability coefficients, and scale determinations available for inspection
constraints: The authors disclaim originality: 'No credit is here given or taken for originality in the formulation of criteria'
Some virtues are superfluous or undesirable for particular uses, e.g. high intelligence correlation is not desirable for mechanical ability tests
target_learners: school students in grades 3 through senior high school
target_learning_goals: measurement of school abilities and capacities such as reading and arithmetic for comparison, experimentation, classification, diagnosis and goal definition
examples: The authors apply the framework to reading tests and intelligence tests, noting that an 'arithmetic' test stressing time may actually measure speed in writing figures
key_sources: Franzen, R., & Knight, F. B. (1921). Criteria to Employ in Choice of Tests. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0075312

article_title: What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks
citation: Rachel Lam. (2019). What students do when encountering failure in collaborative tasks. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0045-1
title: Nine-category coding scheme for dialogic behaviors within micro-failure episodes
description: The article developed and validated a coding scheme for student behaviors during micro-failure episodes in collaborative dialog. As reported, "We identified nine categories of behaviors that occurred within failure episodes in the dialogs: questioning and explaining with a partner, explaining after teacher prompts, arguing to consensus, initiating teacher help, making a quick choice without consensus, arguing without consensus, quick arguing with a dominating partner, ignoring contributions and moving forward, and going off task." Two raters independently coded 20 percent of episodes with sufficient interrater agreement (κ = 0.72, P < 0.01), and the scheme underpinned the Functional/Dysfunctional grouping and all subsequent analyses.
requirements: Verbatim transcripts of student dialogs; micro-failure episodes segmented by overt displays of impasse (uncertainty, disagreement, questioning, pauses, hedges)

description: A 62-item questionnaire combining a 14-item Feelings toward Biology section from Russell and Hollander (1975) with a modified Students’ Attitudes Towards science scale (SATB) from Glynn (2007), whose 8 sub-scales (48 questions) cover general interest, motivation, benefit and utility, career motivation, self-efficacy, self-determination, grade motivation, and assessment anxiety. The article used it as the dependent measure, administered online via Qualtrics on a five-point Likert scale, with anxiety items reverse-scored. The article reports "Internal consistency reliability for each factor was higher than 0.7".
